**Surat al-Mumtahanah**

Its central theme is the disavowal of those who profess faith from those who are marked by hostility, as proof of the soundness of their claim, just as the disbelievers disowned the believers and denied the truth that had come to them, so that they would not be more eager for their falsehood than the believers are for their truth. Its name, al-Mumtahanah (the one tested), is the clearest and most indicative feature of it, because marriage ties are the greatest of connections and the most honourable of them after religion. When these are negated and forbidden, this indicates the greatest severance, because it signifies the debasement that comes from disbelief, which is the foulest of disobedience.

**In the name of Allah**, the Sufficient for whoever takes refuge in Him, for whoever commits himself to Him is made independent of all others.

**The Most Merciful**, whose bounty of existence encompasses all who brought being out of non-existence and originated them, and whose mercy of clarification embraces all whom He endowed with intellect and sustained.

**The Most Compassionate**, who singles out with success whom He loves and approves.

* *

Since discipline following bounty is worthy of acceptance, and He, glorified is He, had established this divine practice, He disciplined His believing servants after the Surah of the Victory (*al-Fath*), which was the cause (of their discipline), with the Surah of the Chambers (*al-Hujurat*). The Surah of Exile (*al-Hashr*) reminded (them) of the bounty in the conquest of the Banu al-Nadir, and taught that there is no guardian except Allah. For this reason He concluded it with the two attributes of might and wisdom, after opening it with them. It is established that wisdom includes the gathering of creation, that the friends of Allah are the successful, and that His enemies are the losers. Love for Allah's sake and hatred for Allah's sake are the best of deeds and the firmest handholds of faith. For this reason He, glorified is He, censured whoever allied with His enemies and supported them, and named them hypocrites despite their profession of the word of Islam. This necessarily yields the obligation to disavow His enemies and to turn wholeheartedly to His service and loyalty. So He said, repeating the discipline after the Surah of the Victory regarding the People of the Book, with a comprehensive surah related to the Greatest Victory and the Victory that was its cause:

﴿O you who believe﴾, addressing them with the particle of distance, although those whose case was the occasion of revelation were among the close ones. He expressed it in the past tense, establishing for him who had shown a kind of friendship to the disbelievers in that situation, stirring him and urging him to rise above it, so that it would not detract from his distinction or lower his high rank, while still showing kindness to him by calling him by the name of faith. Whereas He, glorified is He, testified against those who did a similar act with the Banu al-Nadir, as hypocrites, and placed them in the position of those who oppose (Him). So He judged the hearts in both places. He said there: ﴿Those who are hypocrites﴾ [al-Hashr: 11], as He says here: ﴿Those who believe﴾.

Since the Surah of the Pleading Woman (*al-Mujadilah*) had previously included a severe prohibition against displaying any affection at all for the disbelievers, and the Surah of Exile included a great rebuke against concealing such affection inwardly, the two surahs together ensured the prohibition of befriending them, outwardly or inwardly. Here He reproached and rebuked whoever professed faith for striving for their affection and exerting himself to obtain it, for that undermines the belief in His singular possession of might and wisdom. Therefore He expressed it in the form of *iftial* (reflexive verb form), and after the rebuke with the vocative particle of distance and the expression with the lowest degree of faith, He said: ﴿Do not take﴾. He added two aspects to this meaning: the expression with that which contains enmity, to make them bold against them and to repel them from them; and the singular form for what is applied to the plural, lest it be thought that what is forbidden is the group bound by the condition of association, and to indicate that they are of one heart in enmity, so the people of truth are more fitting to be the same in loyalty. So He said: ﴿My enemy﴾, meaning, while you claim to be loyal to Me [and it is well known that a friend of an enemy, even at the lowest level of friendship, is not a true friend, so how about what is above the lowest level]. It is *fa'ul* from *'adā* (to be hostile), and more emphatic in awakening with His words: ﴿and your enemy﴾, meaning the most intense in enmity toward you, so long as you oppose him in religion.

Since He used the singular for the reasons already mentioned, indicating the unity of the word, He clarified that the intended meaning is the plural, and so He said: ﴿Friends﴾. Then He resumed explaining this unity with His words, pointing to the extreme of haste and eagerness in this matter, through the expression ﴿you throw﴾, meaning all that is in your possession, which you do not hope to keep, like throwing a heavy object from a height, ﴿to them﴾, despite their distance from you physically and in meaning, ﴿with affection﴾, [meaning] by means of it.

When the listener expected an explicit statement of their opposition in the quality by which He had addressed them after having alluded to it, He said, stirring and inciting them to enmity toward them, by reminding them of their opposition to Him in belief, which implies their belittling, because that is the greatest opposition: ﴿And they have disbelieved﴾, meaning, while the state is that they have disbelieved, meaning they have covered over all the proofs you possess ﴿with what﴾, meaning because of what ﴿has come to you of the truth﴾, meaning the matter that is established and perfect in its stability, of which nothing is more stable. Then He resumed explaining their disbelief with what keeps away even the basic affection toward them, let alone striving for it, by saying, reminding them of their past state to increase the aversion from them, and depicting it with what indicates persistence: that they ﴿expel the Messenger﴾, meaning the one perfect in messengership, whom every person is obliged to oppose even at the lowest level of enmity toward whoever opposes him, even if he were the closest of people, so how much more so when he is an enemy. He also clarified that the addressees at the beginning of the surah were among the emigrants, and that its address in the plural form was for the sake of travelling (p-٤٨٧) and generalising in the prohibition, with His words: ﴿and you﴾, meaning from your homelands, from the honoured city of Mecca.

When He had clarified their disbelief, expressing it in the present tense to indicate the continuance of their harm to those who believed, which required their leaving their homeland, He gave the reason for the expulsion with what realises the meaning of disbelief and enmity, and so He said: ﴿that﴾, meaning they expelled you from your homelands for the sake of ﴿you believing﴾, meaning that you bring into being the reality of faith with renewal and continuance.

Since belief in Him, glorified is He, is deserved from both aspects, of His essence and of His attributes, He turned the address from the first person to the third person to alert to both, and so He said: ﴿in Allah﴾, meaning the One singled out with all the attributes of perfection. When He expressed what showed that He is deserving of belief for His own essence, He followed it with what requires that belief be due to His beneficence, and so He said: ﴿your Lord﴾. When He had stirred them against their separation from them by what they had done to them, and the purpose of alerting them through the context of the third person had been fulfilled, He returned to the first person, because it is more endearing, greater in winning affection, and more indicative of approval. So He stirred them by what had come from their side of that [action], that they should not neglect it, and so He said, informing them that His guardianship, glorified is He, is valid only with faith, and faith is established only with its evidences from deeds, and deeds are valid only with sincerity, and sincerity is not attained except by disavowing the enemies: ﴿If you have been﴾, meaning firmly, at the time they expelled you from your homelands for the sake of your belief in Me, ﴿you have gone forth﴾, meaning from them, though they were the most beloved lands to you, ﴿in struggle﴾, meaning for the sake of striving ﴿in My way﴾, meaning for the sake of your intention to ease the path I have prescribed for My servants to follow, ﴿and seeking My pleasure﴾, meaning and for the sake of your seeking with the greatest desire My pleasure, and for every act that is a place for it. The answer of this condition is omitted, because of the indication of ﴿Do not take﴾ upon it.

When He had finished clarifying [the state of] the enemy and stipulated the sincerity of the friend, and the implicit meaning was: "So do not take them as friends", He built upon it His words explaining ﴿you throw﴾, informing that confiding a secret to someone in which there is benefit is only an expression of affection: ﴿you confide﴾, meaning you bring into being the confiding of everything that indicates advising them and showing affection toward them. He pointed to their distance from them with His words: ﴿to them﴾, to emphasise the rebuke by indicating that they undertake this exertion, seeking to convey the news that the Prophet ﷺ, who is supported by revelation, wanted to conceal from them, in a secret manner, for fear of exposure, and to convey it to a distant place ﴿with affection﴾, meaning by means of it, or by means of informing them of news intended by it or that necessarily entails affection.

Since the intent of confiding secretly is concealment from one who dislikes it, He said, rebuking whoever does it: ﴿And I know﴾, meaning while the state is that I ﴿know﴾, meaning more than anyone, from the very nature of the doer, ﴿what you have concealed﴾, meaning of that, ﴿and what you have made public﴾. So what is the benefit of your secrecy if you know that I know it? And if you imagine that I do not know it, then that is the crushing blow.

Since the implicit meaning, indicated by the conjunction, was: "Whoever among you does this has thought (p-٤٨٩) that I do not know the unseen, or has done what requires that thought", He joined to it His words: ﴿And whoever does it﴾, meaning brings into being the taking [of them as friends], secretly or openly, or brings into being the confiding of affection. Public display is more fitting at any time, whether past, present or future. Since the lover may do, out of presumption upon the other's affection, what merits rebuke, when he is rebuked he thinks that this is not its true meaning, because his love is not harmed by anything. And since He had concealed the faults by phrasing the speech in general terms, He declared explicitly that this reproach is intended as a token of love, and so He said: ﴿from among you﴾. He confirmed and drew near the matter with His words: ﴿has indeed strayed﴾, meaning has lost his way, deviated and erred, ﴿from the even way﴾, meaning from the straight, broad and expansive path leading to the upright, just aim and its justice.

The occasion of revelation of this verse has been narrated through many channels. Some of it is in the Sahih from Ali, and some of it in al-Tabarani from Anas, and some of it in the books of tafsir: that Sarah, the freedwoman of Abu 'Amr ibn Sayfi ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf, came to Medina while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preparing for the conquest of Mecca. He asked her what had brought her, and she said: "My patrons have died and I am in severe need, and you are my family, my kin and my patrons." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib and the Banu al-Muttalib, and they gave her, clothed her and provided her with a mount. Then Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, an ally of the Banu Asad ibn 'Abd al-Uzza, wrote with her: "From Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to the people of Mecca: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intends you, so take your precautions." He gave her ten dinars. (p-٤٩٠) Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with the news, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Umar, 'Ali, 'Ammar, al-Zubayr, Talhah, al-Miqdad and Abu Martha, and they were all horsemen. He said: "Set out until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a woman with a letter from Hatib to the polytheists. Take it from her and let her go her way. If she does not hand it over to you, strike her neck." So they set out, their horses racing with them, and they overtook her at that place. She denied it and swore by Allah. They searched her but did not find it, and they were about to return. Then 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We have not lied, nor have we been lied to," and he drew his sword and said: "Bring out the letter or I will strip off your clothes and strike your neck." She said: "On condition that you do not send me back." Then she brought it out from her braided hair, which she had wound her hair around, and they let her go. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Hatib: "Do you recognise the letter?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What moved you to this?" He said: "Do not hasten, O Messenger of Allah. By Allah, I have not disbelieved since I embraced Islam, nor have I been deceitful since I advised you, nor have I loved them since I parted from them. But no one among the emigrants was without someone in Mecca through whom Allah would protect his kin, and I was a stranger and an ally among them, and my family were among them, so I wanted to gain a favour with them by which Allah would protect my family. I know that Allah, the Exalted, will bring His might upon them, (p-٤٩١) and that my letter will not avail them anything." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "He has spoken truly. Say nothing to him except good." Then [Umar] ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "What do you know, O 'Umar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do what you will, for I have forgiven you.'" Then the eyes of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, overflowed, and he said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as friends﴾ "...

…the verses."

Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: This surah (meaning this surah) opens with the command to the believers to abandon *muwalah* (taking allies and loyal friends, i.e., allegiance) with their enemies, forbidding them from that and [commanding them] to disassociate themselves from them (*tabarru'*). This is the meaning found in His words at the end of al-Mujadilah: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], up to the end of the surah. It has resulted [from these surahs] that the most sublime states of the people of faith and their highest ranks are ﴿those in whose hearts He has written faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. So He commanded His servants at the opening of al-Mumtahanah to keep themselves free from allegiance to the enemies, and He admonished them with the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and those who were with him, in their disavowal of their people and their enmity toward them. The connection in this is clear. It seems that surah al-Hashr came as a parenthetical digression, intended to prepare the discourse and alert the listener (p-492) to what completes the benefit of what was mentioned: that it is the nature of the believers not to love those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are the closest of people to them. [The surah] digressed to declare Him free of their misdeeds, then followed that with what He hastened for them of vengeance and punishment. Then the matter returned to the prohibition of allegiance to the enemies in general. Then, since the beginning of al-Mumtahanah was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, may Allah be pleased with him, and his letter to the disbelievers of Quraysh in Makkah, and the story is well known, and the disbelievers of Makkah were not from among the Jews, and they all sought enmity (toward the believers), it is one matter. Therefore [the surah] made distinct what completes the report about the condition of the Jews. At that point the discourse returned to the command concerning their counterparts among the stubborn disbelievers. The three surahs are interlinked, and in surah al-Mumtahanah the repetition of commands and covenants is abundant. The aim of all of this, and for this same reason, [the surah] mentions the ruling on the pledge of allegiance of women and what is required of them in that regard. So the foundation of the surah is the demand for fulfilment, at its beginning and its end, as has been explained in the tafsir, so that it may keep the believer free from the condition of those whose mention came earlier in surah al-Hashr [and] at the end of surah al-Mujadilah. Ended.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 2:

Since what Allah Most High had made clear about their expulsion of them, demonstrating their enmity, and since their restraint from aiming harm at them lasted from the year of the Confederates (sanat al-Ahzab), the year five, until the year eight, it might have led some to doubt its reality. Glorified is He, who had granted might to the believers after their humiliation, strengthened them after their weakness and frailty, and made them knowledgeable after their ignorance, He clarified the shadow of the belief in that by stating that the restraint of the disbelievers is only due to their incapacity, and that if they were to acquire the strength that the Muslims now possess, they would hasten to display enmity. Yet that would be in the service of Satan, so the friends of the Most Merciful are more deserving of following what He has given them of faith. So He said, explaining that their enmity remains: ﴿If they overcome you﴾, that is, find you at some time and in some place while they hope to seize you, being stronger than you or more knowledgeable of what leads to victory. By the particle of doubt (in) He indicated that their finding you while in a state of being in control is something unattainable; it is only by way of supposition and assumption. He, glorified is He, knows that if it were to happen, how it would be, even though it is something that will not happen. He alerted to their deep-rootedness in enmity by the use of the verb "to be" (yakunu), so He said: ﴿they will be to you﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿enemies﴾, that is, they will run toward harming you with every kind of enmity they are able to, even if you love them.

And since enmity may come about through incitement by others, He made known that, because of the intensity of their rage, they do not limit themselves to that, so He said: ﴿and will stretch out to you﴾, that is, specifically, even if at that time there are among others those who killed the dearest of people to them, ﴿their hands﴾, that is, by striking, if they are able, ﴿and their tongues﴾, that is, by insulting, combined with the action of their hands, like one whose chest is constricted by what he has swallowed from another, from others besides you, of stories, until it obliges him to the utmost expansiveness, ﴿with evil﴾, that is, with everything that is of a nature to cause harm.

And since the greatest of enemies toward you is one who wishes to deprive you of the most precious things you have, and since the most precious thing for everyone is their religion, He said, completing the explanation: ﴿and they wish﴾, that is, this wish had already arisen from them before this, because the calamity to religion is greater [so they are quicker to it, because the custom of the enemy is to aim at the greatest harm he sees for his enemy], and He expressed it with what conveys the wish that occurs in impossibilities, so that the meaning is that they loved that intensely and wished for it; and in this is good news that it is of the category of the impossible: ﴿that you would disbelieve﴾, that is, that disbelief which entails everlasting perdition would occur from you. He put the first first because it is clearer in enmity, even though the second is more painful.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 3:

Since their enmity was well known, and only the love of kinship concealed it (for love of a thing blinds and deafens), He criticized their opinion in befriending them by informing them of their own states. He made them lose interest in it by showing what befalls those for whose sake they befriended them, namely the lasting misery that such friendship brings on the Day of Resurrection. So He said, beginning a new statement to inform them that this is an error in every state: ﴿Your relatives will not benefit you﴾, meaning in any way [of the ways] ﴿nor your children﴾, meaning your kinship ties that move you to (p-495) mercy toward them and affection for them. ﴿Nor your children﴾, who are the closest of your relatives, if you befriend the enemies of God for their sake. Therefore you should not consider their nearness to you to count in any way at all. Then He gave the reason for this and clarified it by His saying: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning the Great Standing.

Since what negates benefit is the occurrence of separation, not that it comes from a particular separator, He said, building the verb for the passive object according to the reading of Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir in most of its transmissions, except that the sad is doubled for emphasis on separation: ﴿He will separate﴾, meaning He will bring about the separation, which is the great severance, through the cutting off of all causes ﴿between you﴾, meaning O people. So He will admit whom He wills of the people of His obedience to Paradise, and whom He wills of the people of disobedience to the Fire. Thus no one will benefit anyone of you in anything at all, unless he came to God [with] a sound heart, and then God will permit his honoring by that.

Since the implied meaning, informing that God is the Separator, the One who harms and benefits, is indicated by the reading of the rest [of the readers], except that Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the fa', and a kasra on the sad, doubled, this is a sign of the greatness of this separation, by its departing from what is customary, returning to the Greatest Name, as a sign of the magnitude of the matter through the dispersal of creatures and their deeds. ﴿So God is competent over that﴾; He joined to it His saying: ﴿And God﴾, meaning the One who has complete encompassing ﴿of what you do﴾, meaning of every deed at every time, ﴿is All-Seeing﴾, so He will reward you for it in this world and the Hereafter. It has passed more than once that (p-496) placing the prepositional phrase first in such a context serves to draw attention to greater care for knowledge of that, not to exclusivity, nor for the sake of rhyme.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 4:

When Allah, glory be to Him, had fully admonished them about that, and His custom was to instruct through the examples of those who came before, this was a place where such an example was expected. So He said, using the particle of expectation (*qad*): ﴿Indeed there has been for you a good example﴾, that is, it has come into existence in complete form. The feminine form of the verb indicates approval of it, even if it was only at the lowest level. ﴿For you﴾, that is, O believers, ﴿an example﴾, that is, a point of emulation, of consolation, of following a precedent and adopting a practice, and a commendable way, ﴿good﴾, one to be desired. ﴿In Abraham﴾, that is, in the statement of the father of the prophets, ﴿and those with him﴾, that is, [among] those before him from among the prophets. Al-Qushayri said: among those who believed in him in his time was his nephew Lot, peace and blessings be upon them both, and they are the exemplars of those who strive (*jihad*) and emigrate (*hijra*). ﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿they said to their people﴾, the disbelievers, though those who believed with him were fewer and weaker than you, while those people were greater in number than your enemies and stronger, and they had kin and relatives among them, and they had hope of reconciliation and of efforts to that end.

Since the weakness they described and the strength of their people would have deterred them from confronting them, they emphasized their statement and said: ﴿Indeed we﴾, that is, without hesitation or doubt, ﴿are free﴾, that is, those who disassociate themselves with a great disassociation, ﴿from you﴾, even though you were the closest of people to us, and we had no helper from them other than you. When they disowned them, they followed this with what was greater in their eyes than them, which is the cause of enmity: ﴿and from what you worship﴾, that is, what you bring into existence as worship at any time in the past, whose expression in the present tense conveys the depiction of a current state, or in the present or the future, whoever it may be. We fear nothing from that, because our God, whom we have severed everything else to turn to, cannot be opposed by anything, and you, with your association of partners with Him, cannot be free of Him.

Since they were polytheists, they said, adding a qualification and clarifying the lowliness of everything else compared to the exalted rank of the one they worship: ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, the Great King, who is sufficient for every Muslim. Since disassociation takes many forms, they specified that it was the comprehensive disassociation of religion that encompasses every kind of disassociation, and so they said: ﴿We reject you﴾, that is, we bring about the covering of everything that ought to be covered, while we deny everything that comes from you, whether religion or otherwise, which entails belief, namely establishing security from denial for whoever informs us of the cause of everything opposed to it, while affirming that. Since the believer has a nature opposed to the nature of the disbeliever, they used an expression that conveys that enmity existed but was concealed. Indicating its strength by the masculine form of the verb, He said: ﴿and there has appeared﴾, that is, it became manifest in a great manifestation. And indicating its magnitude by the omission of the preposition, to show that it fills everything between the two parties, He said: ﴿between us and you﴾, that is, in the totality of the dividing boundary between each one of us and each one of you, ﴿enmity﴾, which is opposition in actions, such that each one attacks the other, and this happens only when rage overwhelms a person, desiring to heal his breast from the intensity of the heat of choking that has befallen him. Enmity is something that extends, so that it fills its container. Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani said in his *Talwih* on the *Tawdih* of Sadr al-Shari'a, at the beginning, in the section on the relations of figurative usage (*majaz*): a verb attributed to a time expression through the implied *fi* (in), without mentioning it, requires that the time be a measure for it, without exceeding it, as in "I fasted the month" (*sumtu al-shahr*), which indicates fasting all its days, unlike "I fasted in the month" (*sumtu fi al-shahr*). So when the verb extends, the time extends with it, to be its measure, and so the day in such phrases as "I became on the day of such-and-such" can be taken in its literal sense, which is that which extends from sunrise to sunset. But when the verb does not extend, such as the occurrence of divorce, the time does not extend, because what is extended cannot be a measure for what is not extended. In that case, it is not valid to take "day" as the extended daytime; rather it must be a figurative usage for a portion of time that is not regarded in common usage as extended, namely *now*, whether it is part of the day or part of the night, as evidenced by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16], since fleeing from the battle is forbidden whether by night or by day. And because the unqualified *now* is a part of the daily *now*, which is a part of the day, so the unqualified *now* is a part of the day, and thus the relation is established.

Since this might be the case for something other than hatred, but rather for discipline or the like, they said: ﴿and hatred﴾, that is, which is opposition in the hearts through great hatred. Since this may pass quickly, they said: ﴿forever﴾. Since this is seen from the improvement of the situation, and it might be for the sake of personal interest, they explained its end in a way by which its cause is known, saying: ﴿until you believe﴾, that is, until you establish security from denial toward the one who commands you to believe and informs you about the Most Merciful, while you are affirming and acknowledging ﴿in Allah﴾, that is, the King who possesses all perfection. Since they believed in Him while also associating partners, they said: ﴿alone﴾, that is, that you deny everything worshipped besides Him.

When the Exalted urged the addressees to take Abraham and those with him as an example in their statement at that time, peace be upon them, He made an exception to it, saying, to comfort the one about whom the story was revealed, and to win his favor, who was Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, may Allah be pleased with him: ﴿except the saying of Abraham﴾, that is, so there is no emulation for you in it, ﴿to his father﴾, promising him before making clear to him that he was firmly an enemy of Allah, the Exalted, because he was sealed upon his heart, so there was no hope of his righteousness. It is said that his father had promised him that he would believe, so he sought forgiveness for him, but when it became clear to him that he would not believe, he disowned him. ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness﴾, that is, I will truly seek forgiveness from Allah, ﴿for you﴾, for this seeking of forgiveness is for a disbeliever, so it is not proper for them to take it as an example in that matter absolutely, without considering that he was sealed upon his heart or was beyond the possibility of return.

Since he promised him forgiveness as an encouragement, he then warned him, lest he abandon striving for salvation, with something whose meaning is: I have in my hand nothing but seeking forgiveness. So He said: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything﴾, that is, since you are a disbeliever, ﴿against Allah﴾, that is, since He is the Supreme King, encompassing all attributes of majesty. He intensified the negation by His saying: ﴿anything﴾. The exception applies to this statement together with the qualification of the combined whole, and it does not require addressing the parts individually. So this clause is not taken in isolation as an exception, because the Prophet (ﷺ), when he called out "Ah, morning!" after the Exalted revealed: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214], would say to each person he named: "I cannot avail you anything against Allah," until he said at the end of that: "O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad! Ask me from my wealth whatever you wish, but I cannot avail you anything against Allah."

When He urged them to take as an example the statement of the sincere ones, and He put first the disavowal, because it is the intended purpose, and made an exception of what should not be emulated, as an interjection between parts of their speech, to show the importance of it, in order to deter from it, He completed what is to be emulated. He said, explaining that they did not proceed to disavow them with what they had said except after they had settled all that they were saying and were content with it, rather than maintaining friendship with them, and that they had devoted themselves to Allah alone with complete devotion, so that He would do with them whatever He wills, whether by letting them overpower them or protecting them from them. But they asked for protection not for its own sake, nor for themselves, but so that this would not increase their enemies in misguidance: ﴿Our Lord﴾, that is, O You who have done good to us by delivering us from destruction through following them, ﴿upon You﴾, that is, not upon anyone else, ﴿we have relied﴾, that is, we did in all our affairs with You the act of one who places his affairs upon a strong one to be sufficient for him, because we know that You suffice whenever You will for every distressing matter, and that whoever You befriend is not humiliated, and whoever You oppose is not honored. We have opposed for Your sake a people who are arrogant and powerful while we are weak, and we are content with whatever befalls us from them, except that Your well-being is wider for us.

Since what befits every person, even if he is a doer of good, is to consider himself deficient and remote from his Lord, because due to the greatness of His majesty no one can measure Him as He deserves, and to resolve to strive in worship, they said, informing about this and counting that resolve as a return: ﴿And to You﴾, that is, You alone and no other, ﴿we have turned in repentance﴾, that is, we have returned with all our outward and inward being. Since the meaning is an explanation, for from You is the origin, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And to You﴾, that is, You alone, ﴿is the final return.﴾

When they informed Him of their submission to Him, glorified is He, and gave as the reason what entails His comprehensiveness, and the combination of all of that entails the most complete praise, from which the request necessarily follows, they stated it explicitly. They said, calling upon Him with the particle omitted to indicate the utmost nearness of He, glorified is He, by reason of the comprehensiveness He possesses: ﴿Our Lord﴾, i.e., O You who nurture us and do good to us, ﴿do not make us﴾ by weakening us and giving power over us, ﴿a trial﴾ (p. 502), i.e., a place of testing, ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾, by punishing us with a punishment that turns us away from what we are upon and turns them away from what they have arrived at, by way of earthquakes because of our Islam, with what necessitates for them the belief that: if You were pleased with our religion, we would be upon the truth and they would be upon falsehood, and You would not have empowered them over us. That would increase them in transgression, supposing that they are upon the truth and we are upon falsehood.

Since the greatest capital of the Muslim is acknowledgment of shortcoming, even if he reaches the utmost in striving, and since God is in the utmost of greatness and the servant is in the utmost of weakness, reaching what is due to Him [what is due to Him], glorified is He, is impossible in any way, they said: ﴿and forgive us﴾, i.e., conceal what we fell short in and efface its trace and its effect. When they asked Him for comprehensive protection from all sides, they gave a reason for it, increasing in humble supplication, submission, and seeking the fulfillment of the request, repeating the attribute of goodness to increase in tenderness and in seeking compassion, by saying: ﴿Our Lord﴾, i.e., the One who does good to us. They emphasized this, informing of the intensity of their desire, with good praise of Him, glorified is He, and acknowledging that they may do something that contains some shortcoming, so that it would be among the deeds of one who [not] knows Him, glorified is He. So they said: ﴿Indeed You, You﴾, i.e., alone, not other than You, ﴿are the Mighty﴾ who overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything, ﴿the Wise﴾ (p. 503) who places things in their most fitting places, so they cannot be overturned. Whoever is like this is worthy of being given beyond what he hoped for and asked.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 6:

When he had completed what urged them to follow the example (ta'assi) of their greatest forefather, because a person's motives to be lenient (mudara'ah) toward someone he fears, whether that person is a relative, a family member, or in any other circumstance, are very strong, especially if the one being dealt with is great, and even more so if there has been a prior friendship and affection between them, then it was fitting that, after the admonition and the consolation, some remnants of that inclination would remain within him. This is especially so since people vary: some are turned back by the slightest admonition, while others need more than that. So he repeated the consolation to reinforce it, in a manner that reached the peak of beauty in encouragement and majesty in warning, and so that it would contain the clearest indication that what lies between them, namely the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), whom they were commanded to follow, including his supplication and other matters, is to be followed without exception, except for what was excepted, so that the desire for it would be intensified. He then began with what indicates an oath, as a sign that whoever does other than this has done a deed of one who denies the excellence of this example. For this reason he mentioned the verb in the feminine form at the beginning: ﴿Indeed there has been for you﴾, that is, O you who claim to have faith. He placed the prepositional phrase first to draw attention to it, saying: ﴿in them﴾, that is, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and those with him, ﴿a good example﴾. He also substituted for ﴿for you﴾ what is decisive in indicating falsehood, saying, pointing out that whoever does not follow their example in this was not hoping for what was mentioned: ﴿for whoever hopes﴾, that is, whoever is disposed to ﴿hope in Allah﴾, that is, the King (p-504) who encompasses all attributes of perfection, so He is the Possessor of majesty who grants protection and is not granted protection against, and of honor, who is worthy of giving everything that is asked of Him, ﴿and the Last Day﴾, on which He will call to account for the smallest and the least of things, and nothing will be hidden from Him. Therefore whoever does not follow their example, his abandonment of following them is evidence of the corruption of his creed, so let him blame no one but himself. Indeed, permission was given to the leader of the Muslims, if he came upon such a person, to punish him, for the knowledge of the unseen that Allah informed our Prophet (ﷺ) of, namely that Hatib (may Allah be pleased with him) had a sound creed and was not deserving of punishment, is cut off with his (ﷺ) death, and does not extend to the rites we established or the proofs we set up.

Since the implied sense was: whoever turns to this following because he hopes in Allah and the Last Day, and so does not incline toward this world, Allah will take him under His care, for Allah is Most Merciful and Most Loving, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾, that is, whoever at any time at all commits aversion from the commands of Allah the Exalted, because he inclined toward this world and did not regard the Last Day, Allah will turn away from him. The form of the verb with the tafa''ul pattern indicates that this does not occur except through the treatment of the original natural disposition (fitrah). He emphasized it because the doer of this is like one who denies the meaning of the statement, so He said: ﴿then indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One who has complete encompassing knowledge and power, ﴿He﴾, that is, exclusively, (p-505) ﴿is the Self-Sufficient﴾, that is, free of need from everything, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, [that is] the One to whom belongs all-encompassing praise, because He encompasses the attributes of perfection, both in the state of obedience to Him and in disobedience to Him. For the disobedient one is a slave to His will, just as the obedient one is a slave to His command, His will, and His kindness. Nothing goes outside His purpose, and everything is subject to His judgment. The verse has explained the etiquette of companionship, since it has stirred and aroused the call to separate from the disobedient and to disassociate from them, both physically and in meaning, and to make this known to them by word and deed, until repentance is achieved. Whoever does not do this becomes a partner in the act and therefore a partner in the consequence, as has been reported. Then this does not prevent him from being a dining companion or a companion in sitting. Allah struck the hearts of some of them against others and cursed them through the tongues of the prophets. Whoever does what Allah commanded him to do, his action is worthy of being a cause of union, closeness, and affection. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned, each one omitted in the other's place): He mentioned hope first as an indication of its opposite second, and turning away second as an indication of its opposite first. Its secret is that He mentioned the cause of happiness as an encouragement, and the cause of misery as a warning.

When he had completed his admonition with what was most beneficial and closest to their righteousness, and they complied, and that was burdensome because of what humans are naturally disposed to, namely love of their kin and tenderness toward them, the souls longed for some kind of relief. So he followed it with a reassurance regarding what Hatib, may Allah be pleased with him, intended, by means other than the way through which it could be reached. He spoke in the manner of kings, who allude to what they want, so that the one promised is content with it. Indeed, that allusion is greater to him than a definite statement from others, because of the greatness that befits them, which requires them to be free from anything that carries a trace of deficiency. This is greater in faith in the unseen, because promises remain between fear and hope. It is an answer to one who seems to say: "How can there be deliverance from such an event, O Lord of this abode, which has been built upon the wisdom of causes?" ﴿It may be that Allah﴾, that is, you are worthy to hope in the King who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿will bring about﴾ through causes you do not know ﴿between you and﴾, that is, in the entire dividing line between the two groups, or between every two persons of the two groups, ﴿those whom you have opposed﴾, that is, through disagreement in religion, ﴿among them﴾, that is, among those who opposed you with what has preceded, individually, from the people of Makkah, ﴿affection﴾. He made that happen in the year of the conquest, realizing what He, glorified is He, hoped for, and He carried out His divine practice that whoever You oppose in it, He makes the outcome of that lead to a great guardianship, and whoever You neglect in opposing Him in it, He, glorified is He, sets up as an adversary for you.

Since the implied meaning was: "So Allah is kind to you," He followed it with a reminder of His greatness, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who has encompassing perfection, ﴿is Powerful﴾, that is, of utmost power over everything He wills. So He has power to turn hearts and make the difficult easy. When hope was complete, nothing remained but the turbidity of sin, so He followed it, to console the hearts regarding what these verses were revealed because of, with: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection ﴿is Forgiving﴾, that is, He erases the very essences of sins and their traces, ﴿Merciful﴾, who honors the sinners when they seek repentance, and then grants them the utmost honor in reward. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "The Prophet ﷺ had appointed Abu Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, over part of Yemen. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away, he came and met Dhu al-Hajjar, who had apostatized, and fought him. He was the first to fight over apostasy." That affection was after enmity.

When the exhortation, consolation, and the easing of hearts with the promise (of reward) were complete, and the description of the disbelievers as those who expel them from their homes could be understood as applying to all of them in potential (bi-al-quwwah), thus being general, or as applying to them in actuality (bi-al-fi'l), thus being specific to the people of Makkah or to those who inflicted the harm that caused their departure, He clarified this by His words, signaling (mu'dhinan bi-al-isharah) moderation in both loyalty and enmity, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Love your beloved moderately, for he may one day become your enemy; and hate your enemy moderately, for he may one day become your beloved."

﴿Allah does not forbid you﴾, i.e., He who is distinguished by majesty and honor, ﴿from those who do not fight you﴾, i.e., actually, ﴿over the religion﴾, i.e., in such a way that you are contained by it, none of their conditions being outside of it. Thus He excluded from this fighting the case of a worldly right that has no connection to religion, and He excluded those who did not fight at all, such as Khuza'ah and the women. Among these are the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah, non-Muslims living under the protection of the Muslim state); indeed, kindness toward them is among the noble morals and lofty qualities, because they are neighbors.

Since those who did not fight might perhaps have assisted in the expulsion, He said: ﴿and did not expel you﴾, and He restricted it by His words: ﴿from your homes﴾. And since He, glory be to Him, had broadened the scope by generalizing the removal of the prohibition, He specified, by His words, in apposition to "those" (of "the religion"): ﴿that﴾, i.e., He does not forbid you from ﴿showing them kindness﴾ through some kind of outward righteousness (al-birr), for that is not explicit in intending affection (al-mawaddah). ﴿And acting justly toward them﴾, i.e., being just in the fullest sense of balance, by removing injustice (al-qast), which is oppression. He clarified that the meaning is: conveying that justice ﴿to them﴾, indicating that the act of justice is included within connection, and that this does not harm them even if they undertake to send things to them from afar, by what is permitted for them in this matter, for that is part of gentleness, and Allah loves gentleness in all matters and rewards for it what He does not reward for harshness.

Then He gave the reason for that by His words, emphasizing it to repel the assumption of one who sees harming the disbelievers in every way:

﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿loves﴾, i.e., acts as one who loves, toward ﴿those who act justly﴾, i.e., those who remove injustice and establish justice.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 9:

Since the situation was known from this and from what came at the beginning of the surah, he followed it with an explicit statement of what it had conveyed in a collected form, in the best gathering and the best depiction. So He, exalted, said: ﴿Allah only forbids you﴾, i.e., He who has complete encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿from those who fight you﴾ deliberately, to fight you, being ﴿over religion﴾; none of that is outside of it, so that the enmity is for the sake of Allah. ﴿And drive you out of your homes﴾, i.e., by their own selves, out of their hatred for you. ﴿And aid [others] in your expulsion﴾, i.e., they assist others. Since this addressed the intended people explicitly, and since the prohibition, whose place is actions, had been attached to their persons as an emphasis for it, he clarified the intended meaning by his saying: ﴿that﴾, i.e., He only forbids you from those mentioned, in that ﴿you make allies of them﴾, i.e., you burden your original natures with doing with them everything that a close, intimate, compassionate relative does, so that you declare them to be your allies and support them, even if that is in the lowest of forms, which is what the dropping of the taa' (in the verb) indicates.

Since the implied sense was: whoever obeys, those are the successful, he followed it with his saying: ﴿And whoever makes allies of them﴾, i.e., burdens his self with inclination toward what his original nature does not call for of opposition; and he stated it without restriction, not qualifying it with "from among you," so that it would include the emigrants and others, and the believers and others: ﴿then those﴾, i.e., those who have strayed far from justice, ﴿they are﴾, i.e., exclusively, not others, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who excel in placing things in other than their proper places, like one who walks in the direction of derivation because of this turning toward them.

When these verses were revealed, concerning the Great Conquest, the Prophet ﷺ set out in the year eight (AH) with the armies of Allah toward the honoured city of Makkah, may Allah honour it, to enter it by force against them, because they had broken their treaty by fighting the Khuza'ah, who had allied themselves with the Prophet ﷺ. They were under his protection and covenant, in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, which took place in the year six and placed the war on hold between them and the Prophet ﷺ and those who entered his covenant. Among the terms of that treaty was that whoever came to the Prophet ﷺ from Quraysh, or entered under their treaty, would be returned to them even if he was a Muslim, while whoever came to them from among those who were with the Prophet ﷺ would not be returned to him. Because of this, many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, rose up and sat down in distress, the greatest of them being 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, until al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, calmed him with the ruling that had settled in his heart. The Prophet ﷺ returned Abu Basir, may Allah be pleased with him, to them. His return was in fulfilment of the covenant, out of belief in the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "As for the one who came to us from them, we returned him to them, and Allah will surely grant him relief and a way out." His story in all of this is well known.

The word "man" (مَن) is among the forms of generality (ṣīghat al-'umūm). The indication of a general term (dalālat al-'āmm) is definitive (qaṭ'iyya) regarding the ruling applied to the individuals, but speculative (ẓanniyya), as al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said, regarding the indication of any particular individual among those individuals, where there is no indicator (qarīna). This is because those forms sometimes come in their general sense, and sometimes only some of the individuals are intended, so they are of the general term intended in a restricted sense (al-'āmm alladhī urīda bihi al-khuṣūṣ). And sometimes specification (takhṣīṣ) occurs within them, so they are of the general term intended in a restricted sense. Thus possibility enters them, and what they indicate of the apparent meaning requires an indicator. The inclusion of women under the word "man" in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah was either devoid of any indicator, or the indicator was the fighting which the treaty was concluded to end, which diverted it from them. Likewise, the indicator is that they (the women) are referred to with "mā" rather than "man" in many places in the Noble Book:

﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [an-Nisa, 3] ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [an-Nisa, 3] ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [an-Nisa, 22] ﴿And the married women, except what your right hands possess﴾ [an-Nisa, 24] ﴿And lawful to you is what lies beyond these﴾ [an-Nisa, 24] ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ [an-Nisa, 24] ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ [an-Nisa, 25] ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun, 6].

He, glory be to Him, concluded these verses, by which He instructed them regarding the conquest, with what clarifies what does not depart from the treaty of the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, of what is closer to goodness than righteousness and justice, and He forbade allying with the disbelievers (tawalli). Marriage and intermarriage are among the greatest forms of such alliance. He connected to this what does not depart from it, and is not made lawful by the covenant: that whoever came from the disbelievers to the Prophet ﷺ was to be returned to them, even if he was a Muslim. So He said, addressing the lowest of the age-groups of the people of faith, who need to be made to understand, while those above them already know this, and by what Allah has given them of understanding, and by the varieties of knowledge with which He illuminated their noble hearts, in order that they might spare the Prophet ﷺ the preliminaries of the pledge from them (the women):

﴿O you who believe﴾, meaning, those who have professed faith, which is the establishment of security from denial, addressing whoever informs them of what ought to be believed, because of their belief in Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

Since He, glory be to Him and exalted, knew that women would come to them fleeing with their religion to Allah, He gave them the good news of this by using the particle of certainty, and said:

﴿When﴾, meaning, having confirmed what you claimed of faith, at whatever time ﴿there comes to you﴾ And since a person does not abandon his home and his kin, especially if they are relatives, because of their disbelief, except one who is firmly rooted in faith, whether male or female, He said:

﴿the believing women﴾, meaning, the women for whom the attribute of faith has become a firmly established quality, as indicated by the emigration:

﴿emigrating﴾ from the disbelievers and from their land. ﴿Then test them﴾, meaning, examine them, as a confirmation of what emigration indicates of faith, by having them swear that they did not leave because of a change they had made, nor out of hatred for a husband, nor desire for a particular man, nor leaving out of love for Allah and His Messenger and desire for the religion of Islam alone. Imam Shihab al-Din ibn al-Naqib said in al-Hidayah, from his abridgement of al-Kifayah by the jurist of the school Najm al-Din Ahmad ibn al-Rif'ah, in his commentary on al-Tanbih:

"The opinion of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, differed on whether the Prophet ﷺ had stipulated to Quraysh in the treaty the return of women. In one opinion, he did not stipulate it, but rather made the return of whoever came to him unrestricted, so they assumed it included women, while the Prophet ﷺ knew they were not included, and so Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him) left it unrestricted. Among his legislation is that war is deception. In another opinion, the stipulation included them. But did he stipulate it explicitly, or did they enter under the unrestricted wording? There are two views, the more apparent being the second. And was their stipulation permissible? There are two views: one says yes, and then it was abrogated (nusikha). Was its abrogation by the aforementioned verse, or was the Prophet ﷺ prohibited from returning them? There are two views based on whether it is permissible to abrogate the Sunnah by the Qur'an, on which al-Shafi'i has two positions. His preferred one is the prohibition, and that is the New (Jadid) view. Likewise, according to him and his followers, it is not permissible to abrogate the Qur'an by the Sunnah, even if it is mutawatir." End of quote.

Its meaning is that this did not happen. If it were abrogated by the Qur'an, there would be a Sunnah with it, and if it were abrogated by the Sunnah, there would be a Qur'an with it. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn al-Subki in Jam' al-Jawami': al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Wherever it occurs by the Sunnah, there is a Qur'an with it, or by the Qur'an, there is a Sunnah with it, a supporting Sunnah which shows the agreement of the Book and the Sunnah."

Since testing may sometimes indicate their faith, which can only be known through it, He negated this by saying, in a new sentence answering one who asks: Is Allah not knowing of this? And indicating that your knowledge which you reach through testing is not true knowledge, but He named it so as a notification that the dominant assumption on your part, arrived at through ijtihad (independent reasoning) and qiyas (analogy), takes the place of knowledge, and comes from Him:

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra, 36]

﴿Allah﴾, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿knows best﴾, meaning, better than you and them, about themselves, ﴿their faith﴾, whether it is present or not, in a firmly established way or not, for He encompasses what is unseen just as He encompasses what is witnessed. He entrusted the matter to you in this only to conceal it from people, and so that His testimony regarding anyone's faith or disbelief would not lead to the certainty of the eye, which would take the matter out of the basis of this world.

Al-Qushayri said: In general, testing is a path to knowledge. The essences of the soul become clear through experience, and whoever embarks on something without trial drinks the cup of regret.

He said: ﴿Then if you know them﴾, meaning, the knowledge that is firmly established for you, which is the strong assumption supported by apparent signs, through the oath and other things, ﴿to be believers﴾, meaning, sincere in their emigration for the sake of faith. The expression of this is for notification of greater caution.

When He mentioned this testing, He explained that it is a cause for protecting them and defending them, so He followed it with its consequence, saying:

﴿Then do not return them﴾, meaning, in any way whatsoever, ﴿to the disbelievers﴾, even if they are their husbands. And among the evidence that this is apparent in what is intended, and that the indicators clarify it, is that when the Prophet ﷺ refused to return to them the women who came to him, none of the disbelievers found fault in this, nor attributed to the time of the Prophet ﷺ — far be it from him — any flaw. Had it not been so, they would have filled the earth with agitation, as they did in the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with him, to Nakhlah, which led to the revelation of:

﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah, 217] and the verses following it. This is so, because the sound reports and others state clearly that this verse was revealed at al-Hudaybiyah, before the matter had reached its complete conclusion and settlement.

al-Bukhari related in the Book of Campaigns (al-Maghazi) of his Sahih, and al-Baghawi from his route, and this wording is his, from al-Marwan and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "He wrote the agreement with Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and among what he stipulated to the Prophet ﷺ was that no one would come to you from us, even if he was upon your religion, except that you return him to us. So the Prophet ﷺ wrote to him according to that. On that day he returned Abu Jandal to his father Suhayl ibn 'Amr. No man came to him except that he returned him during that period, even if he was a Muslim. The believing women came as emigrants. Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt was among those who came out to the Prophet ﷺ while still a young woman. Her family came to Madinah asking the Prophet ﷺ to return her to them, but he did not return her to them, as Allah had revealed concerning them: ﴿When believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them﴾."

Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out as one performing 'Umrah, until when he reached al-Hudaybiyah, the polytheists of Makkah made a treaty with him that whoever came to him from the people of Makkah he would return to them. Then Subay'ah bint al-Harith came as a Muslim after the completion of the writing of the agreement. Her husband came, and he was a disbeliever, and said: 'O Muhammad! Return my wife to me, for you have stipulated that you would return to us whoever comes to you from us, and this is the ink of the agreement which has not yet dried.' So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them. Allah knows best their faith﴾."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Their testing was that they be made to swear that they did not emigrate out of hatred for a husband, nor out of passion for a man among the Muslims, nor out of desire to leave the land, nor because of a change they had made, nor seeking worldly gain, and that they came out only out of desire for Islam and love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear this, and they swore, and he did not return them. He gave their husbands what they had spent on them, and he married her to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. The Prophet ﷺ used to return the men who came to him, but would detain the women who came to him after testing them, and he would give their husbands their dowries.

The claim of abrogation (da'wa al-naskh) is nothing, except that it is interpreted as follows: since this is of the general term intended in a restricted sense, some of what the apparent wording of the expression included of the ruling is lifted. This is because Allah does not command the breaking of a promise, so how could He command the breaking of a covenant?

When He forbade returning the emigrants to the polytheists, and expressed it with "disbelievers" in a generalised way, He gave the reason for it, by saying, putting their ruling first as an honour for them because of their emigration:

﴿They are not lawful to them﴾, meaning, the husbands, ﴿lawful﴾, meaning, a place of lawfulness that is established ﴿for them﴾, meaning, for the disbelievers, whether by enjoyment or otherwise.

Since the negation of an established lawfulness does not prevent the renewal of the men's lawfulness for them, even under some supposition or hypothetical assumption, He said, repeating this and emphasising the severing of the relationship from every side:

﴿Nor are they lawful to them﴾, meaning, the disbelieving men, ﴿they cannot become lawful﴾, meaning, it does not renew at any time that they become lawful ﴿to them﴾, meaning, to the believing women, even if it were imagined that their husbands were women and they were men, they would not be lawful to them. This is unlike the People of the Book. Likewise, the connection is dissolved in the matter of zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce by likening a wife to a mother) and ila' (a vow to abstain from intercourse), so that it is lawful for the woman to enjoy him if he is asleep, for example, while it is forbidden for him to do so before expiation. al-Baydawi said: The first (negation) is for the sake of the occurrence of separation, and the second is to prevent resumption. End of quote. So this nominal sentence negates in one respect the renewal of lawfulness for the women, and the two clauses together convey the absence of blame for what occurred before this, as a comfort to the hearts of the believing women.

When He forbade the return and gave its reason, He commanded what He had already mentioned of giving justice to them:

﴿And give them﴾, meaning, the husbands, ﴿what they spent﴾, meaning, on their wives, of dowries, for the dowry is in return for the basic companionship and its continuance, and the emigrant has forfeited that, so the loss of the marriage and the loss of property are not combined upon him. As for the maintenance and the expenditure, these are for what is renewed over time.

Then, having firmly decreed that they (the women) be withheld from the disbelievers, He permitted them to the Muslims, saying, in a manner of gentleness and kindness: ﴿There is no blame﴾, i.e., no inclination and no sin (ḥaraj), ﴿upon you﴾, O you who are honoured with address, ﴿that you marry them﴾, i.e., that you renew your marriage with them after the waiting period (istibrā'), even if their husbands were among the disbelievers and had not divorced them, because the bond (ʿalaq) has ceased from them concerning them, and because Islam has separated between them; for Allah will never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers.

And since He had commanded the return of the disbelievers' bridal gifts, one might have thought that this sufficed to dispense with giving them a new dowry (mahr) when a Muslim marries them, so He negated that by saying: ﴿when you have given them their due bridal payments﴾, i.e., for the sake of marriage (nikāḥ), ﴿their ujūr﴾. Then, since He had severed what lay between the disbelievers and the Muslim women, together with turning away from the disbelievers because of their disobedience, He severed what lay between the believers and the disbelieving women, together with turning toward them because of their obedience, as an elevation of their status, and He said: ﴿And do not﴾. And since retaining a woman despite her enmity, because of her opposition in religion, is a proof of the utmost desire for her, He indicated this by a hint of reproach through the doubling of the letter in the reading of the people of Basra (p-519), so He said: ﴿hold on to﴾, i.e., by not explicitly divorcing, ﴿the bonds of disbelieving women﴾, plural of ʿiṣma (bond), which is that which maintains the tie of marriage (ʿalaqat al-nikāḥ). ﴿And ask back﴾, i.e., O believers whose wives have gone over to the disbelievers, ﴿what you have spent﴾, i.e., of the bridal gifts of your women who have withdrawn their bonds from you with them, or who fled to them.

And since He had commanded the return of the believers' bridal gifts to the disbelievers, and had permitted the believers to claim the bridal gifts of their wives, He permitted the disbelievers the same, establishing justice among His servants, both Muslim and disbelieving, expressing it as a command with the third person, turning away from them, to inform of the intensity of His dislike of injustice, and that in this the disbeliever is equal with the believer, despite his enmity versus the believer's allegiance: ﴿And let them ask back﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿what they have spent﴾, i.e., of the bridal gifts of their wives who have embraced Islam and withdrawn their bonds from them to you. Whether this ruling remains in force: some people said yes, while ʿAṭā', Mujāhid and Qatādah said it was abrogated (nusikha), so that the disbelievers are not given anything, even if we stipulated the giving.

And since this is a just ruling which none would enact toward his enemy and his ally except a Wise One, He said, pointing to its praise and encouraging adherence to it, with the plural suffix (mīm al-jamʿ) indicating generality: ﴿That is﴾, i.e., the ruling mentioned in these verses, which is exalted in rank above all folly, ﴿the judgement of Allah﴾, i.e., the King who possesses the attributes of perfection, so no flaw should attach to Him. (p-520) And since this is something one rejoices in and is grieved to see lost, He said, resuming, to give good news of the continual renewal of the like of it for them: ﴿He judges﴾, i.e., Allah, or His judgement, by way of emphasis, and this indicates that judgement encompasses everything that arises among the servants, and that He, glorified, has not neglected any of it, through the omission of the preposition in His words: ﴿between you﴾, i.e., in this time and at other times, in this excellent manner. This was for the sake of the truce (hudna) that took place between the Prophet ﷺ and them; but before Ḥudaybiyya, the Prophet ﷺ would retain the women without returning the dowry.

And since the implication is: "Allah is a just Judge," He said: ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs complete encompassment, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of perfect knowledge, nothing hidden from Him, ﴿All-Wise﴾, i.e., because of the completeness of His knowledge He perfects all His affairs with the utmost perfection, so no one can undo any part of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 11:

Since it was presumed of the disbelievers that they would not act justly, so that they would not give the believers the dowries of their disbelieving wives, He said, treating that disease: ﴿And if any of your wives have gone over to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., by escaping from you after the emigration (hijrah), or by continuing to reside in the lands of war, ﴿some [of your wives] have gone over to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., whether little or much, ﴿from among your wives﴾, i.e., from their persons or from their dowries, ﴿to﴾, i.e., while separating from you or arriving at ﴿the disbelievers﴾, so that you were unable to recover it, ﴿then you retaliate﴾, i.e., you become able to exact retaliation, by the loss to the disbelievers of something of their wives through their emigration to you, or you seize [something] from the wives of the disbelievers, so that the turn of your victory comes, ﴿to pay﴾ the dowry to your brethren, obediently and justly, following their turn in which they appropriated what you had spent, through disobedience and injustice. ﴿Then give﴾, i.e., bring forward and give from the dowry of the emigrant women, ﴿to those whose wives have gone﴾, i.e., from among you, if they choose to take it, ﴿the equivalent of what they had spent﴾ on the disbelieving woman who went over to the disbelievers, from the goods of theirs that you have seized, or by your giving them the equivalent of the dowries of their wives, from what you used to give to the wives of the emigrant women; this will be a recompense and retaliation for what the disbelievers did.

Since partial division in such a matter is difficult for the soul, for dowries vary at times and are equal at other times, and at times are in money and at other times in goods, and so on through other conditions, and since the one dealing is an enemy in religion, justice in this matter will not be borne except by pure piety, He said: ﴿And fear﴾, i.e., in giving and withholding and otherwise, ﴿Allah﴾, who possesses the attributes of perfection, and He has commanded you to take on His attributes to the extent you are able. Then He described Him with what emphasizes the difficulty of the matter and urges justice, saying, stirring them up completely and shaking them by the description of firmness in faith: (p-522) ﴿in whom you are﴾, i.e., specifically, ﴿believers﴾, i.e., firmly established in the rank of faith.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 12:

When He, glorified is He, had addressed the believers, to whom belongs the role of defence, protection and support, regarding what He had settled for the believing women in the abode of the Hijrah (emigration), and the test took place and faith was recognised, He commanded the Prophet ﷺ, after the ruling on their faith, to take their pledge (bay'ah). So He said, ﴿O Prophet﴾, addressing him with the description that calls for knowledge, and the particle of confirmation indicates that what he is informed of, namely their coming, is certain, as one of the signs of prophethood. So He said: ﴿When the believing women come to you﴾, making their coming to him ﷺ, especially with the Hijrah, the justification for applying the description to them, ﴿pledging allegiance to you﴾, meaning each one of them pledges, ﴿that they will not associate anything with Allah﴾, meaning that they will not commit association with any of the existing things at any time, ﴿Allah﴾, meaning the King who has no equal, ﴿anything﴾, meaning any kind of association whatsoever.

Since association is the giving of the King's right to one who does not deserve it, He followed it with taking the property of the owner without right, because the situation calls for it, given the woman's ability to embezzle her husband's property and the difficulty of guarding against her in that. So He said: ﴿and that they will not steal﴾, meaning they will not take the property of another without entitlement, secretly. He then followed this with giving another's right to one who is not its owner, so He said: ﴿and that they will not commit adultery﴾, meaning they will not allow anyone to have intercourse with them without a valid contract.

Since adultery may be a cause of bringing into existence or destroying a soul without its right, He followed it with the destruction of (p-523) a soul without its right, so He said: ﴿and that they will not kill their children﴾, meaning by burying them alive, as was mentioned in Surah al-Nahl, and whether that child is from adultery or not.

Having mentioned the destruction of a soul without right and without legitimate cause, He followed it with what includes bringing a soul into existence without lawful basis. He said, censuring it by way of metaphor, with slander and what accompanies it, by portraying it through its consequences and effects, because recalling the ugly and depicting its form is more effective in deterring from it. So He said: ﴿and that they will not bring a slander that they have invented between their hands and their feet﴾, meaning a child from other than the husband, whose attribution to him would astound him with perplexity in denying it, ﴿that they invent﴾, meaning they deliberately lie about it. He clarified the intended meaning and depicted it by saying: ﴿between their hands and their feet﴾, meaning through pregnancy in the wombs, ﴿and their feet﴾, meaning through birth from the private parts. And because the custom of a child, though it falls between the hands and feet of its mother, is that it walks before her. This includes whatever arises from doubt or from a found child.

Having clarified these grave major sins, magnifying their matter because of the difficulty of avoiding them, and having emphasised the prohibition of adultery by direct correspondence and by implication, since what leads to it includes killing and whatever is lesser, and having stressed the matter of lineage because of what branches from it of creating doubts (p-524) and violating sanctities, He made the prohibition general, so He said: ﴿and that they will not disobey you in what is reputable﴾, meaning in any circumstance whatsoever, ﴿in any reputable matter﴾, any single instance of it, whether small or great. In mentioning it, together with the knowledge that he ﷺ commands only what is reputable, there is an indication that there is no obedience to any created being in disobedience to the Creator. He placed the prohibitions before the commands derived from "reputable," because abandoning vices precedes adorning oneself with virtues, since averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits. ﴿So accept their pledge﴾, meaning commit yourself to them to what you have promised concerning that, namely giving reward to those among them who fulfil it in return for what they have bound themselves to of obedience. Since man is a place of deficiency, especially women, He gave them hope with His saying: ﴿and ask forgiveness for them from Allah﴾, meaning ask the Greatest King, Lord of Majesty and Honour, for forgiveness should any shortfall occur from them, and it does occur, since no one can estimate Allah as He truly deserves to be estimated.

Since His greatness, glorified is He, prevents, because of the awe of His majesty, asking Him for what He has encouraged, He gave the reason for it with His saying, repeating the Greatest Name lest it be supposed that its omission and its restriction to the circumstance of the Hijrah applies to women and the like, emphasising what the human being is naturally disposed to, namely that he hardly leaves the offender without punishment or reproach, let alone favour through increased honour: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the One who possesses the attributes of majesty and honour. Were people not to sin (p-525), He would bring forth a people who sin, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them, so that the attribute of His honour might appear. ﴿Is Forgiving﴾, meaning reaching the utmost in covering sins, both in their essence and their effect, ﴿Merciful﴾, meaning reaching the utmost in honouring after forgiveness, by His grace and kindness. Glorified is He, He has realised that and spoken truly, and who is more truthful in speech than Allah? "The women came to pledge allegiance generally on the second day of the Conquest, at Safa, after the Prophet ﷺ had finished taking the pledge of the men. This verse was revealed while he was at Safa. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, stood below him, taking their pledge by his command and conveying his words to them. Hind bint ʿUtbah was veiled and disguised among the women, for fear that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ might recognise her. When he mentioned association, she said: 'By Allah, you are indeed demanding of us a matter which we have not seen you demand of men,' and the men had pledged that day to Islam and jihad. He said, ﴿and that they will not steal﴾. She said: 'Abu Sufyan is a stingy man, and I take some of his property, small amounts, and I do not know whether that is lawful for me or not.' Abu Sufyan said: 'Whatever you have taken of anything in the past and in what is to come, it is lawful for you.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed, and recognised her, and said: 'Are you Hind bint ʿUtbah?' She said: 'Yes, so pardon me for what has passed; may Allah pardon you.' He said, ﴿and that they will not commit adultery﴾. She said: 'Does a free woman commit adultery?' He said, ﴿and that they will not kill their children﴾. She said: 'We raised them as little ones, and you killed them as adults, and you and they know best.' Her son Handhalah ibn Abi Sufyan had been killed on the day of Badr. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, laughed until he lay back, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled. He mentioned slander, which is that a woman attributes to her husband a child that is not his. Hind said: 'By Allah, slander is indeed ugly, and you only call us to right guidance and noble character.' He said, ﴿and that they will not disobey you in what is reputable﴾. She said: 'We have not sat in this gathering of ours with any intention of disobeying you in anything. The hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ never touched the hand of a woman who was not lawful to him.' Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan was among those who pledged, and she said: 'O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, extend your hand that we may pledge to you.' He said: 'I do not shake hands with women, but I take their pledge by word.'" And on the authority of al-Sha'bi: "The Prophet ﷺ called for a vessel of water, dipped his hand in it, then the women dipped their hands in it." And on his authority: "The Prophet ﷺ taught them in the pledge: 'in what you are able and capable of,' and they said: 'Allah and His Messenger are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves.'"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 60, verse 13:

When He had mentioned what He commanded His Prophet ﷺ regarding the pledges, after counting those who believed as the foundation in the testing of the women emigrants, it became known from this that accepting the women as allies, although there is no harm from them through fighting or the like, is not permissible except after knowledge of their faith. And since closing the surah with the attributes of forgiveness and mercy had emboldened the believers to show favouritism toward some of the disbelievers, whether wives or others, on account of kinship or other ties, for a reason the husband puts forward or other such matters, He, glorified is He, repeated the command to disavow every enemy, returning the end of the surah to its beginning, as an emphasis on turning away from them and a warning against their allegiance, as the verse of the pledge and the verse of the testing had conveyed. So He said, delighting them with address that turns them toward Him, just as He did at its beginning with the sweetness of reproach: ﴿O you who believe﴾.

Since inclination away from the straightest path, contrary to what the primordial nature commands, does not occur except through neglecting it, He expressed it with the reflexive form (tafa''ul), just as He expressed it at the beginning of the surah with the ifti'al form, and said: ﴿Do not take as allies﴾, meaning, make an effort to restrain yourselves from taking as allies ﴿a people﴾, meaning people who have strength in what they attempt, so others are a fortiori included ﴿with whom Allah is angry﴾, meaning the Sovereign Most High has brought down anger ﴿upon them﴾ because of their turning to what sins have surrounded them with. It is general for everyone who is characterized by this, and it primarily includes the Jews.

Since the hearer of this expects an explanation of the cause of the anger, He said, giving the reason and clarifying that there is no good in them to be hoped for, even if something contrary to that appears: ﴿They have despaired﴾, meaning they have certainly lost hope ﴿of the Hereafter﴾, meaning that any good from it will reach them, either because their sins have surrounded them or because they do not believe in its occurrence. Whoever allies with them is about to be counted among them, and so anger will settle upon them ﴿as the disbelievers have despaired﴾ of attaining good from it ﴿of the companions of the graves﴾. Since whoever dies and becomes fit for burial has the conditions of the Resurrection revealed to him, so he knows whether he is saved or destroyed, and since the dead are more general than the disbelievers, and the dead disbelievers are more general than those of them who are buried, He said: (p-528) ﴿of the companions of the graves﴾. For the disbelievers among them have known their despair of attaining good from it with certain knowledge.

It is also possible that "min" is for the beginning of the source, and the meaning would then be: as the worshippers of idols have despaired of meeting one who has died and been buried, believing that there is no reunion between them at all, because he cannot be resurrected either to this world or to the Hereafter, since for them there is no Hereafter at all, especially if he is buried in a grave. In this case the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that what made them despair is the concealing of the proofs despite their clarity, had they been fair. So do not take as allies one with such a description, for between you and him will be what is between a relative and his relative, in that each of them turns to the other with what a close friend turns to his relative. For their alliance is harm with no benefit in it, since whoever is angered by the Sovereign, the Witness over every movement and stillness of his, neither prospers himself nor does whoever allies with him. The least harm in his allegiance is that the help in it is cut off, and the partnership through death; and even if it is after death, a partnership is in the enduring, continuous punishment that does not cease for them, and the abiding disgrace. It is known that this last is the first of it, and this is what connects its details. So glorified is He who sent it down as a Book that is miraculous and wise, and a Qur'an that is concise, comprehensive and magnificent.
